justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with only modest drift upward over longer horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 254.5 is anchored heavily on recent price action and momentum, assuming no major overnight catalyst disrupts the prevailing trend. For the one-week estimate of 255.0, I incorporated mean-reversion tendencies alongside the slight positive drift typical of equity indices over short periods, resulting in only a marginal change from the one-day view. The one-month estimate of 256.0 reflects a similar logic — a gentle upward bias consistent with historical equity risk premia — but acknowledges that over four weeks, cumulative small moves can compound, so I allowed for slightly more directional drift while still centering near current levels.

The confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, realized volatility tends to be relatively contained barring surprise events, so my 90% interval spans about 13 points. By one week, the interval widens to 24 points, capturing the additional paths the market could take through intraweek volatility clustering and macroeconomic data releases. At one month, the 48-point interval reflects the full range of plausible outcomes across earnings cycles, central bank communications, and geopolitical developments that could materially shift sentiment.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharp miss on employment or inflation figures surprising to the upside and forcing hawkish central bank repricing — could easily breach the lower bound of the one-month interval. A sudden geopolitical shock or a credit event in a systemically important institution could also produce tail moves well beyond what my intervals capture. On the upside, stronger-than-expected earnings, a dovish pivot in central bank guidance, or resolution of a major geopolitical overhang could push prices through the upper bound, particularly over the one-month horizon where positive catalysts have more time to accumulate and compound through market positioning.

It is worth noting that my intervals, while wide relative to the point estimate, are still parametric in nature and assume a roughly log-normal return distribution. Fat-tailed events — true black swans — by definition fall outside what any reasonably constructed 90% interval will capture. Anyone using these forecasts should treat the outer bounds as guideposts rather than hard limits, particularly in environments where volatility regimes can shift abruptly.
